exp: Binary insertion sort uses binary search to find the insert position in O(log n), but still has to shift up to O(n) elements per insertion, so the overall worst-case time stays O(n^2) even though comparisons drop.
A node whose value exceeds everything in its left subtree and is less than everything in its right subtree, applied recursively, is exactly the binary search tree property.
Bubble sort is the slowest of the four listed in typical practice, with O(n^2) comparisons and swaps and no divide-and-conquer or gap-based speedup like the others have.
Add/remove restricted to one end only (LIFO) is the definition of a stack.
With an adjacency matrix, the degree of a vertex is found by scanning its entire row (or column) of n entries, i.e. O(n).
Trees are acyclic by definition, so 'a tree contains a cycle' is the false statement; the other three (n-1 edges, connected, bipartite since no odd cycles) are all true of trees.
A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no cycle of odd length.

This describes the AVL balance condition (left/right subtree heights bounded within one of each other); the wording 'differ at least by one' is almost certainly a printing slip for 'differ by at most one', but AVL-tree is still unambiguously the intended answer among these options.
A complete binary tree where every parent's value is >= its children's values is, by definition, a max-heap.

The classic textbook figure for a shortest-path algorithm (e.g. Dijkstra) using an adjacency-matrix implementation is O(n^2); with an adjacency list and a priority queue it would instead be closer to O(e log n), but O(n^2) is the answer this style of question is built around.
The whole point of a hash table is average-case O(1) lookup, unlike the O(log n) or O(n) costs of tree- or list-based searches.
Sorting is, by definition, rearranging a collection of records into a specified order by key.
Comparing each pair of adjacent elements and swapping them when out of order, repeated over the list, is exactly bubble sort.
In a full binary tree, leaves = internal nodes + 1, so with n leaves there are n-1 internal nodes and n + (n-1) = 2n-1 nodes total.
With n non-leaf (internal) nodes, a full binary tree has n+1 leaves, giving n + (n+1) = 2n+1 nodes total.
Building a tree where every node is larger than everything in the subtree beneath it, then repeatedly removing the maximum, is the heap-sort technique (a max-heap).
Merge sort's worst case is O(n log n) because it always splits evenly and merges linearly; insertion sort, bubble sort, and quicksort (worst-case pivot choice) all degrade to O(n^2).
The first dimension -1..m holds m+2 values (from -1 up to m inclusive) and the second dimension 1..m holds m values, so the array holds (m+2)*m = m(m+2) elements.
Binary search needs O(1) random access to the middle element at each step, which a linked list can't provide without an O(n) traversal, making it unsuitable for that use.
Inserting a record into a circular linked list typically means relinking two 'next' pointers, the new node's own next pointer and the previous node's next pointer, so 2 pointers are modified.

A linked list is a dynamic structure that grows/shrinks at run time; option (b) contradicts itself (static yet variable), and a stack can in fact be implemented with a linear linked list, so only (a) is true.

The minimum-node AVL tree of height h follows N(h)=N(h-1)+N(h-2)+1 with N(0)=1, giving N(1)=2, N(2)=4, N(3)=7, so 7 nodes is exactly enough to reach height 3 but not height 4 (which needs 12), making 3 the maximum achievable height.
In any full binary tree the leaf count is always one more than the internal-node count, so 10 leaves forces exactly 9 internal nodes and 19 nodes total, regardless of shape.

The number of structurally distinct binary trees with 3 (unlabeled) nodes is the Catalan number C3 = 5, which isn't among the printed options (12-15) at all; this looks like a transcription error, possibly confusing it with C4 = 14 for 4 nodes. Picking 14 as the closest plausible intended value, but this question has no verifiably correct option as printed.

Because B+-tree leaves are linked together in sequence, range queries (scan from a start key to an end key) are faster on B+-trees than on B-trees, where you'd have to do repeated in-order traversal hops.
A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem is the standard definition of an algorithm.

A structure that captures adjacency, each element having a well-defined 'next' neighbour, is what makes a data structure linear (arrays, linked lists), as opposed to hierarchical (tree) or networked (graph) structures.
Array elements are stored in contiguous (successive) memory locations, which is what enables O(1) index-based access.

The sentence needs two answers to fill its two blanks, row major and column major (options C and D), but the output format only allows a single letter, so this can't be answered correctly as a single-choice question; picking C (row major) as the primary one, but D (column major) is equally required.
Counting only the top-level elements of ((5,6), 0, (9,6,3,5)), the pair, the 0, and the 4-tuple, gives a length of 3.

List A = (a, A, a) contains itself as an element, so expanding it recursively never terminates, giving it (conceptually) infinite length, a classic example used to illustrate recursive/self-referential list structures.
In a max-heap the greatest key is always stored at the root, since every parent is >= its children.
A B-tree is defined so that all of its leaves sit at the same level, which is what keeps it balanced; ordinary binary/AVL trees don't guarantee this.

Merge sort and heap sort both always take O(n log n) regardless of input, so their best and worst cases coincide; insertion sort (paired with merge sort in option b) does not share this property since its best case is O(n).
Selection sort always performs exactly n-1 swaps no matter the input, so it's preferred when swapping large records (large values) is expensive but comparing small keys is cheap.
Quicksort partitions the array around a pivot and recursively sorts each half, the textbook definition of divide and conquer.
Building a heap bottom-up (Floyd's build-heap) takes O(n) time overall, not O(n log n), because most nodes near the bottom need very few sift-down steps.
Converting a recursive algorithm to an iterative one typically requires an explicit stack to manually track the state the call stack would otherwise hold.
Peek (or top) returns the value at the top of the stack without removing it, unlike pop which removes it.
Every recursive function call is pushed onto the call stack, making recursive function calls a canonical stack application.
Array elements are accessed via their index/position, which maps directly to an offset from the base address.

Across most mainstream languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C++ std::string, etc.) the '+' operator is the common way to concatenate strings, though a few languages (e.g. classic BASIC/VB) use '&' instead.
Bitwise manipulation operates on raw binary representations of numbers, not on the character-level operations (concatenation, comparison, substring) that strings support.
A bit field is a structure member (or variable) declared to occupy a specific, often sub-byte, number of bits, letting several small values pack into one word or byte.
